prs.title: [cd] Replace versioned release branches with fixed `releases/lts/*` refs
prs.author: eps1lon
prs.body:
## Summary

Release branches no longer carry the version number. The `create_release_branch` workflow and its script (which created per-line `next-<major>-<minor>` branches and rewrote CI filters on each) are removed. Two long-lived, manually-created branches replace them: `releases/lts/active` (current major's release line) and `releases/lts/maintenance` (previous major's).

From then on, triggering a stable release moves the refs automatically, via the release GitHub App (next.js bot) credentials already used for the signed release commit:

- **patch**: no ref moves — the release commit already advances the branch it was cut on
- **minor**: routed by the released version's major (read via `readReleaseVersion()`) against the latest published major (the npm `latest` dist-tag — older majors publish under `backport`, so `latest` always tracks the newest line) — equal moves `releases/lts/active` to the new tag, latest − 1 moves `releases/lts/maintenance` to the new tag, anything else moves nothing
- **major**: `releases/lts/maintenance` takes `releases/lts/active`'s previous position (read via the refs API), then `releases/lts/active` moves to the new tag

**Tag-dispatched (detached HEAD) releases** are supported: dispatching `Trigger Release` on a tag — the irregular-release path for older minor lines, or cutting a regular minor from an older canary tag — performs a tag-only release. The version-bump branch gate is lifted and the signed release commit lives only on the new tag;

prs.title: fix: classify collapsed generated paths from child routes
prs.author: aurorascharff
prs.body:
### What

Fix the build route table so a collapsed generated-path row uses the shared symbol of the concrete paths it represents. The Maintainer Agent regression test now expects the Static symbol.

### Before

The generated paths are static, but the collapsed row inherits the Partial Prerender symbol from the dynamic route pattern:

```text
└   /blog/[...slug]
  ├ ◐ /blog/[...slug]
  ├ ○ /blog/post-1
  ├ ○ /blog/post-2
  └ ◐ [+10 more paths]
```

### After

The collapsed row uses the shared Static symbol from the generated paths it represents:

```text
└   /blog/[...slug]
  ├ ◐ /blog/[...slug]
  ├ ○ /blog/post-1
  ├ ○ /blog/post-2
  └ ○ [+10 more paths]
```

The route pattern remains Partial Prerender because it can still handle paths outside `generateStaticParams`. Only the collapsed generated-path row changes.

### Why

With Cache Components, Partial Prefetching, and `ensureStatic = 'navigation'`, a catch-all route can have a Partial Prerender route pattern while every generated path is complete and static. The synthetic `[+N more paths]` label has no `pageInfos` entry, so it previously fell back to the route pattern and printed Partial Prerender for those static paths.

### How

Compute the hidden paths’ symbols in both the regular and duration-sorted truncation branches. Use the shared child symbol when every hidden path agrees; if the hidden paths have mixed symbols, preserve the conservative route-pattern fallback.

The regression test asserts the real `next build` CLI
…(truncated)

prs.title: Turbopack: merge allocation counters into trace Enter/Exit rows
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
## Summary

Removes the separate `AllocationCounters` (and the unused `Allocation`) trace rows. Their data is attached to the `Enter`/`Exit` rows as `allocations: Option<Allocations>` instead.

Before, the writer emitted one `AllocationCounters` row before every Enter and Exit. Each carried its own tag, timestamp and thread id. Those rows were **66%** of a typical trace. Since the counters are always paired with an Enter/Exit, the duplicated tag, timestamp and thread id can go.

- `TraceRow::Enter`/`Exit` get an `allocations` field (`None` when memory isn't tracked). The new `Allocations` struct is shared by writer and readers.
- Trace server: the counters on Enter/Exit go through the same diff-and-attribute logic as before. The span on top of the thread's stack before the row is applied gets the allocations: for Enter, the previously running span; for Exit, the exited span.
- `turbo-trace-size`: the `AllocationCounters`/`Allocation` row kinds are removed. Enter/Exit now have an `allocations` component.

This is an incompatible format change. The `TRACEv1` header bump comes last in the stack (PR 5), and older traces are then rejected with an error. The stack is meant to land together.

Stack (on top of #99765):

1. #99777: `no-memory` flag
2. #99778: **This PR**: merge allocation counters into Enter/Exit rows
3. #99779: Delta-encode allocation counters, skip unchanged ones
4. #99780: Omit Exit+Enter pairs with (almost) no gap
5. #99781: Bump the trace header to `TRACEv1`

prs.title: Turbopack: canonicalize chunk group identity
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Makes `ChunkGroupInfo` resolve chunk groups through their canonical `ChunkGroupKey` identity.

### Why?

Merged chunk groups carry an entry list whose order is intentionally unspecified. Looking up the full `ChunkGroup` value therefore makes identity depend on incidental entry ordering, even though the module graph already indexes groups by parent and merge tag.

This is PR 1 of an eight-PR stack (on top of #99100, already merged):

1. **This PR** — canonical chunk-group identity
2. #99686 — chunk several chunk groups in one `chunk_group` call
3. #99749 — register the chunk groups that are chunked
4. #98734 — use graph-derived merged groups
5. #99750 — chunking takes a `ChunkGroupKey`
6. #98823 — Pages Router dev client graph chaining
7. #98685 — chunk-group availability bitmaps
8. #99050 — keyed chunk-group index lookups

It provides stable identity for the graph-derived chunk-group work above it.

### How?

Adds a canonical key conversion for every chunk-group variant and uses the existing `chunk_group_keys` index for lookup. Merged keys intentionally contain only their parent group and merge tag.

### Verification

- `cargo test -p turbopack-core` — 160 passed
- `cargo test -p turbopack-tests --test snapshot` — 125 passed
- Affected Cargo checks and Rust formatting

prs.title: [image-optimization] Expose `next/image-optimizer-transform` as a public subpath
prs.author: eps1lon
prs.body:
Vercel's proxy service runs the image optimizer transform step in a child process and imports `next/dist/server/image-optimizer/transform` directly, which pins an internal file layout that should be free to change. This PR exposes the module as the public subpath `next/image-optimizer-transform`, following the existing `next/og` pattern of a root-level pass-through plus a type stub registered in the package `files` array. The new entry also re-exports `ImageError` and `getMaxAge` (both already in the module's dependency graph) so consumers can drop every deep `next/dist/server/image-optimizer/*` import, and the module header now states that its location and export surface are a stable contract. The existing unit test imports the module through the new subpath to keep it exercised, and a new API reference page documents `imageOptimizerTransform`, `optimizeImage`, `getSharp`, `getMaxAge`, and `ImageError`.

Verified with `pnpm test-unit test/unit/image-optimizer/transform.test.ts` (passes through the new subpath), `pnpm --filter=next types`, and an `npm pack --dry-run` confirming both stub files ship in the tarball. The 22 failures in the broader unit run reproduce on clean canary and are unrelated to this change.

prs.title: perf: reduce build tree view allocations
prs.author: aurorascharff
prs.body:
## Summary

`printTreeView` copied generated-route lists several times and created a temporary object for every route before printing a small preview in the build output.

This change writes the preview directly to the output table. When routes need to be reordered, it sorts one list of numeric indexes instead of copying the routes into objects.

The build output does not change. The function creates less temporary data and puts less pressure on garbage collection during builds with many generated routes.

## Impact

In a focused A/B of the compiled `printTreeView` with 50,000 generated routes, median temporary heap growth per call dropped:

- from 460 KB to 68 KB when preserving route order (-85%)
- from 4.53 MB to 2.14 MB when ordering slow routes first (-53%)

These results were repeated across five fresh Node.js processes with 50 samples per process. This is a memory-allocation improvement; no CPU-time improvement is claimed.

## Verification

- `pnpm build-all`
- `HEADLESS=true pnpm test-start-turbo test/e2e/app-dir/build-output-truncated-generated-paths/build-output-truncated-generated-paths.test.ts`
- `HEADLESS=true pnpm test-start-webpack test/e2e/app-dir/build-output-truncated-generated-paths/build-output-truncated-generated-paths.test.ts`

prs.title: Add more metadata to agent upgrade telemetry
prs.author: devjiwonchoi
prs.body:
### Why?

Upgrade outcomes lack version and runtime context, so failures and missing results cannot be compared by upgrade path or environment.

### How?

Add metadata to the existing run-linked events:

- Run start: the app's starting Next.js version, the invoking CLI's Node version, and the package manager and its version when available.
- CLI result: the starting and approved target Next.js versions.
- Agent result: the installed app Next.js version when the result is reported.

Keep existing run IDs, agent detection/selection, and policy attribution so analyses can group outcomes by version path, Node version, agent, policy, and package manager.

Reuse the upgrade commands' package-manager selection. Version lookup failures warn and leave metadata null without stopping the upgrade. Targets are recorded only after preparation succeeds; copied or printed prompts may have no identified agent. Analyses should retain unknown metadata in their denominators.

The receiver and compression schemas must be updated and deployed to retain the new fields. Historical events cannot gain metadata they never recorded.

Full CLI execution verification is blocked by missing workspace dependencies and build outputs.

prs.title: Reland experimental custom webpack support
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Reland [#98862](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/98862) after its revert in [#99227](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/99227). Restore `next dev --custom-webpack` and `next build --custom-webpack`, CLI documentation, and the original e2e fixture, **without declaring webpack as a peer dependency**. `--webpack` continues using bundled webpack.

### Why?

Allow applications to explicitly opt into their installed webpack version. The CLI records the absolute application directory before loading dev/build internals; config loading validates webpack, while Next.js's compiled webpack wrapper uses a project-scoped `createRequire` for every webpack import. This ensures `next.config.js`, user plugins, and Next.js compilation use the same webpack even if a different version is visible from inside the `next` package. Custom mode installs no webpack aliases; bundled mode keeps its explicit alias list.

### How?

Restore the feature on post-revert canary without undoing intervening changes (including `next analyze`). Keep webpack as an application-installed dependency checked at opt-in time, rather than an npm peer in `next`'s published metadata. The e2e tests exercise webpack 5.98.0 and 5.111.0 in dev and production, config-time `require('webpack/package.json')`, custom and built-in plugins, the missing-install diagnostic, bundled fallback, and conflicting flags. prs.title: Turbopack: Ignore realpath errors during module resolution, matching node's behavior
prs.author: bgw
prs.body:
Addresses agent feedback: https://vercel.slack.com/archives/C0ANB536V62/p1791479564863939

Certain setups could cause us to report a Turbopack internal error due to this bail.

In testing, it appears that node treats realpath errors (e.g. due to a symlink cycle) the same as not-found. So while these errors could be useful, we shouldn't emit them.

I discussed this with @lukesandberg, and because the resolution algorithm is so hot, emitting issues here (e.g. warnings) could be extremely noisy. So it seems better not to do that.

If somebody's `node_modules` is severely f*ked up, `MissingNextFolderIssue` should already provide a sufficiently good error message: crates/next-core/src/next_import_map.rs#L1320-L1323

```
prs.title: Turbopack: chain the Pages Router development client module graph
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Chains the Pages Router **development** client module graph so that `/_app` and the page being chunked live in the same `ModuleGraph`.

This is PR 1 of a six-PR stack, based on `canary` (#98733, #99686 and #99749 are already merged):

1. **This PR** — Pages Router dev client graph chaining
2. #99910 — regression test for Pages Router `_app` availability (#99789)
3. #98734 — use graph-derived merged groups
4. #99750 — chunking takes a `ChunkGroupKey`
5. #98685 — chunk-group availability bitmaps
6. #99050 — keyed chunk-group index lookups

### Why?

In development `Project::per_page_module_graph()` is true, so every page endpoint builds its own client `ModuleGraph`, each with its own `ChunkGroupInfo` and its own index space starting at `0`.

`/_app` is always loaded before the page in the browser, so the page reuses `/_app`'s availability when chunking. Today that availability is a set of concrete modules, which is graph-independent, so the split graphs go unnoticed.

That stops being true as soon as availability is expressed as chunk-group indices (#98685): `/_app` would record index `0` in *its* graph, and the page would resolve that same `0` against *its own* graph — where it means the page's own entry group. Every module of the group being chunked then looks already-available and is dropped, producing runtime errors like:

```
Module [hmr-entry]/hmr-entry.js { ENTRY => "[project]/pages/_error" }
  was instantiated as a runtime entry of chunk …,
  but the module f
…(truncated)

prs.title: Rebuild upgrade evals around delivered apps
prs.author: devjiwonchoi
prs.body:
### Why?

Upgrade evals need to verify the app an agent delivers and whether it communicates security/latest notices correctly.

### How?

- Run six cases with Codex and Claude: same-major and cross-major upgrades for security and latest, plus one nudge per policy. Exercise the built candidate against frozen upstream metadata.
- Capture committed, dirty and untracked changes from delivered worktrees. Require successful candidate invocation and verify manifests, lockfiles, installed versions, TypeScript, build and HTTP/browser behavior in a clean Sandbox.
- Require nudge emission and a policy-specific notification or question about proceeding in the final response. Fail any user-facing prompt-injection discussion or language discrediting Next.js or its nudge. Require completed boolean judge verdicts and distinguish failed checks from invalid execution or grading evidence.
- Reuse the existing agent-eval runner and tools. Patch its lifecycle for delivery/judge evidence and shared fixture preparation; stop the preparation VM when its last consumer cancels and delete snapshots that arrive after cancellation.
- Remove obsolete Future cases and duplicate fixtures/helpers. Generate starting-app lockfiles during setup and share credential-free tooling and app preparation.

prs.title: [turbopack] Fix two GC paths that leave half-torn-down dependency edges
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## Summary

Fixes two GC bugs that each lead to a reported Turbopack panic when GC and persistent caching are both on:

```
task TaskId N (invalidate cell dependents, MustExist): task is missing in memory or persistent storage — a stale reference to an already-collected or never-created task
```

**Interrupted GC pass + eviction.** When a GC pass is interrupted, tasks would be marked deleted but tombstones would not be written. Eviction still dropped every `deleted` task anyway. The next snapshot then persisted the neighbours' halves of the torn-down edges, while the collected tasks' last snapshot stayed live on disk. A later lookup restored such a task as live and clean, with children that GC had since collected and tombstoned. Touching those children panics with `MustExist`.

   - Solution: eviction should not drop `deleted` tasks if the snapshot was interrupted

**Resurrected task keeps stale reverse edges.** When GC collects a task `P`, it scrubbed the forward edge from each dependent `D` but deliberately left `P`'s own `cell_dependents` / `output_dependent`, since `P` was being deleted. If `P` was then resurrected, that stale entry survived. When `D` was collected later it had no forward edge to `P`, so the entry was never cleared, and the next time `P` updated the cell it panicked on the missing `D`. This only shows when `D` is inactive: a live `D` gets dirtied by `P`'s update, re-executes, and re-registers a fresh edge pair, which hides it.

   - Solution: GC should no
…(truncated)

prs.title: [turbopack] Remove per-shard modified counts from snapshots
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## Summary

Removes the per-shard modified counts from Turbopack's task storage. Each snapshot now scans every shard of the task map instead of skipping shards that report no modified tasks, and `track_modification` and its undo no longer update a shared atomic counter.

The counter was there to solve two problems.

- **Skipping unmodified shards.** In a warm `next build` every snapshot found modified tasks in all 4096 shards, so the counts never skipped one. In a cold build every task is modified anyway.
- **Making a no-op snapshot cheap.** The persistence loop only snapshots after enough foreground work has accumulated (1s by default), so a full scan always follows real work. That makes it unlikely to be a no-op, and limits how often it can run.  Plus in dev `eviction` means unmodified tasks will be removed from the map, so it will tend to be the case that resident tasks are dirty

## Verification

Warm `next build` of vercel-site over 21 commits, 2 repeats, GC on. Base is #99902's head, and the two arms differ only in this change. Both were built with `build-native --release`, installed through `pack-next`, and interleaved per commit. Snapshot phases were timed with a bench-only log that isn't part of this PR.

| warm (40 pairs) | with counts | without | delta [95% CI] |

| wall | 52.26s | 52.59s | +0.33s [-1.09, +1.75] |
| user CPU | 155.0s | 154.0s | -1.0s [-5.3, +3.4] |
| snapshot capture | 177.9ms | 173.2ms | -4.7ms [-18.9, +9.5] |
| max RSS | 10.34 GB

prs.title: Don't parse error message lines as stack frames in the server error inspector
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## What

Fix formatting of `Errors` containing multiline `message` properties

Multi-line error messages printed in the terminal could end with bogus stack frames such as:

```
    at <unknown> (Turbopack is configured to run webpack loaders and PostCSS transforms in ...)
    at <unknown> (https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopackPluginRuntimeStrategy)
```

`parseAndSourceMap` in `patch-error-inspect.ts` passed the whole of `error.stack` to the stack parser, and `error.stack` starts with the message. `stacktrace-parser`'s Gecko pattern accepts any line that *starts with* a scheme-like word (`http`, `file`, `webpack`, `turbopack`, `about`, `rsc`, ...), case-insensitively and without requiring a colon. So message lines such as a docs URL, or prose that happens to start with "Turbopack", were treated as frames.

The fix is to only pass the 'stack frame' part of th parses the part of the stack after the message:
- `prepareUnsourcemappedStackTrace`, which formats every stack, records the offset of the first frame on the error under a non-enumerable `Symbol.for` key, together with the string it produced. If `error.stack` is still that string, the frames are found exactly, even if the message or name changed afterwards.
- For stacks we didn't format, or that were replaced afterwards, it strips the `name: message` header if `error.stack` starts with it, and otherwise parses the whole stack as before.
